content:
According to a joint status report released earlier, Apple said it is still waiting for Jon Prosser to provide additional documents and hopes to take Michael Ramacciotti's deposition again; the two defendants have also raised objections to the way Apple is handling the case. Details are as follows.

According to a joint status report submitted to Judge James Donato, disputes over who is responsible for the delays are intensifying between Apple, leaker Jon Prosser, and Michael Ramacciotti in the trade secrets lawsuit Apple filed against the two in July 2025.

A bit of background

In short, shortly after unveiling iOS 26, Apple filed a trade secrets misappropriation lawsuit against Prosser and Ramacciotti, stemming from a video Prosser posted disclosing multiple system details, including the ultimately confirmed major visual overhaul, Liquid Glass.

Apple alleged that Ramacciotti improperly obtained a developer's iPhone from a later-terminated employee and showed Prosser, via FaceTime, unreleased iOS features running on the device.

Since then, the case itself has seen plenty of dramatic developments, including a default judgment entered against Prosser by the court clerk for failing to timely respond to Apple's complaint (though Prosser countered that he had not ignored the case).

Roughly eight months later, the court agreed to set aside the default judgment and gave him another chance to formally answer the allegations.

Court filings show that, on the other hand, Ramaciotti has answered Apple's complaint and has largely complied with its document production requests.

However, since Prosser hired a lawyer and formally joined the lawsuit, the situation has deteriorated sharply, with the three sides increasingly pointing fingers at one another over who should be held responsible for the alleged trade secret disclosures and the subsequent delays.

The latest joint status report

Returning to the latest status report, Apple said it wants Ramacciotti to update his written discovery responses and sit for a deposition again, in order to address what it described as inconsistencies with "Mr. Prosser's testimony."

However, Ramacciotti said he is willing to sit for another deposition as long as Apple provides "a roadmap explaining the direction of its case on the relevant claims, including exactly what it still needs from him (if anything)."

As for Prosser, Apple said it is "still waiting on some of the additional documents requested more than three months ago, including earnings reports and analytics for his YouTube channel and communications with third parties identified during his deposition."

Prosser countered that "the trade secrets at issue in this case no longer appear to be trade secrets and have entered the public domain." In other words, his argument appears to be: since Apple has publicly released the iOS update featuring Liquid Glass, the information at the core of the case is now public and no longer meets the definition of a secret.

As part of the joint status update, Ramacciotti asked the court to hold a status hearing this month, during which Apple must specify what additional information it still needs from him. He also wants Apple to have 30 days at that point to either voluntarily withdraw its claims against him or commit to taking the case to trial.

Meanwhile, Apple wants to continue the document discovery process, including taking Ramacciotti's deposition again and compelling Prosser to produce the documents he has not yet provided. Prosser, for his part, maintains that he has fulfilled his document production obligations under the parties' agreement and is resisting Apple's ongoing further requests.

If Judge Donato does not grant Ramacciotti's request for a status hearing, the parties have suggested submitting another joint status report on December 2.
